The Me I Show Online

Welcome! In this learning unit you are going to explore the way you live online — what you scroll through, what you share, and what your phone really knows about you.

Over three sessions you will read, listen, talk and create. By the end, you will have produced two pieces of work that you can be proud of:

  • An interactive infographic with practical advice for healthier digital habits.
  • A short podcast in English in which you have a conversation with… your own phone.

Both products will be shared with the rest of the class through Microsoft Teams, so you will get to see and hear what your classmates have created too.

Take your time, enjoy the topic, and don't be afraid to be honest about your own digital life. That's where the best ideas come from. 📱

By the end of this learning unit, you will be able to:

  • Talk and write about your digital habits using vocabulary related to mobile phones, social media and the Internet.
  • Understand authentic spoken and written texts about technology and well-being at a B1.2 level.
  • Give advice and recommendations using a range of structures (you should…, why don't you…, it's a good idea to…, try …-ing).
  • Plan and design a clear, attractive infographic in English.
  • Plan, script and record a short podcast in English with appropriate intonation and natural turn-taking.
  • Reflect critically on your own relationship with technology.

Warm-up Questions

Before we begin, take a moment to think honestly about these questions. There are no right or wrong answers — just be honest with yourself.

  1. What is the first thing you do in the morning? And the last thing at night?
  2. How many hours a day do you think you spend on your phone? Check your screen-time settings now and compare. Were you right?

Are You Doomscrolling? Three Digital Habits That Are Hurting You

Your phone is probably the first thing you touch in the morning and the last thing you see at night. That alone is not a problem. The problem is what you do during those minutes — and during all the other minutes in the day when you pick up your phone "just for a second" and end up scrolling for half an hour.

Researchers have given names to three of the most common digital habits that, in small doses, are harmless, but that can seriously affect your well-being if they get out of control.

1. Doomscrolling

Doomscrolling is the habit of spending a long time scrolling through bad news. You start by checking the headlines and, twenty minutes later, you have read about a war, a fire, an accident and a celebrity break-up. You feel worse, but you can't stop. Why? Because your brain is looking for safety: "if I keep reading, I will understand the world and feel in control." Unfortunately, the opposite happens — you feel anxious and powerless.

2. FOMO (Fear Of Missing Out)

FOMO is the uncomfortable feeling that everyone else is having a better time than you. You see your friends at a concert, on a beach, at a wedding — and you are at home folding laundry. The truth, of course, is that they are also at home most of the time, but they only post the highlights. FOMO can make you say yes to plans you don't really want, and feel guilty when you say no.

3. Social comparison

Social media platforms are designed to show you the best version of other people: their nicest holidays, their funniest jokes, their most attractive photos. After half an hour of scrolling, it is easy to feel that your own life is boring or that you are not good enough. This is called upward social comparison, and studies have shown that it is linked to lower self-esteem, especially in young adults.

What can you do?

The good news is that you don't need to throw your phone away. Small changes — turning off notifications, leaving the phone in another room at night, unfollowing accounts that make you feel bad — can have a big effect. The first step is simply noticing what you are doing. That is what this unit is about.

  1. To check knowledge of core course concepts (this could be a pre-check, formative exercise, or summative check).

Language for Advice
Giving advice in English

When you write your infographic, you will need to give clear advice. There are many ways to do this in English. Here are the most useful structures at B1.2 level:

1. Modal verbs

  • should / shouldn't + infinitive (without "to") — the most common way to give advice.
    You should turn off your notifications at night. / You shouldn't check your phone at the dinner table.
  • ought to + infinitive — slightly more formal than "should".
    You ought to take a digital break every weekend.
  • had better + infinitive — stronger advice, with a sense of warning.
    You'd better stop scrolling if you want to sleep tonight.

2. Suggestions and recommendations

  • Why don't you + infinitive? Why don't you leave your phone in another room?
  • How about / What about + -ing? How about deleting the app for a week?
  • Try + -ing. Try setting a daily time limit on Instagram.

3. Imperatives — short and powerful

Imperatives are very common in infographics: Turn off notifications. / Don't check your phone before sleeping. / Set a screen-time limit.

4. Useful expressions

  • It's a good idea to + infinitive.
  • It helps to + infinitive.
  • One way to … is to + infinitive.

⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

  • ✗ You should to turn off notifications. ✓ You should turn off notifications.
  • ✗ Why don't you to delete the app? ✓ Why don't you delete the app?
  • ✗ How about to leave the phone outside? ✓ How about leaving the phone outside?

A great infographic doesn't happen by accident. Follow these steps to plan yours.

Step 1 — Choose your angle (5 min)

Choose ONE of these focuses:

  • "5 tips for a healthier social media diet"
  • "How to stop doomscrolling tonight"
  • "The phone-free morning: a 7-day plan"
  • "How to unfollow without guilt"
  • Your own idea — discuss it with your teacher first.

Step 2 — Write your 5 tips (15 min)

Write 5 short, clear tips. Each tip should:

  • Use one of the structures from Language for Advice.
  • Be no longer than 12 words.
  • Include a verb of action.

Step 3 — Decide on visuals (5 min)

For each tip, think of: an icon and a colour (pick 2–3 colours maximum).

Step 4 — Add an interactive element

Your infographic must have AT LEAST ONE interactive element: clickable button, hover effect, animation, or embedded video/audio.

Starting a conversation

Write Your Script
Your script: step by step

Duración:
40 min
Agrupamiento:
Individual

Now it's your turn. Follow this template to write your own script (around 250–300 words = 2–3 minutes when read aloud).

Structure

  1. OPENING (1 turn each) — Greet your phone and announce the topic.
  2. FIRST QUESTION OR COMPLAINT (2–3 turns) — You bring up something that bothers you. Your phone defends itself.
  3. DEEPER EXCHANGE (2–3 turns) — Use vocabulary from this unit (doomscrolling, FOMO, screen time…).
  4. ADVICE / DEAL (2 turns) — Use "how about…", "why don't you…", "you should…", etc.
  5. CLOSING (1 turn each) — End with humour or a memorable line.

Tips

  • Give your phone a personality. Sarcastic? Polite? Tired? Anxious? Pick one and stick with it.
  • Read your script aloud BEFORE recording. If a line feels strange, change it.
  • Don't write big paragraphs — short, real-sounding sentences work better.
  • Add small interjections: "Hmm…", "Well…", "You know what?"

Record Your Podcast
Recording guide

Duración:
30 min de aula + casa
Agrupamiento:
Individual o parejas

Option A — Record both voices yourself (recommended)

Record yourself reading both parts. Change your tone, your speed and your distance from the microphone for each character.

Option B — Record with a partner

If you have a classmate, friend or family member willing to play "the phone", record together.

How to record

  1. Use Vocaroo (vocaroo.com) — free, no installation, in your browser.
  2. Or use the Voice Memos app on your phone.
  3. Or use Audacity on your computer (free, open-source).

Find a quiet room. Get close to the microphone (15–20 cm). Don't shout — speak at a normal volume.

Editing (optional but recommended)

  • Cut long silences.
  • Add a short intro music (Bensound or YouTube Audio Library — both free).
  • Add a tiny sound effect (a phone notification at the start).

Whatever tool you use, export/save your final file as .mp3.

screen timeThe total time you spend looking at a screen each day.

algorithmThe system that decides what content you see on social media.
